AI advances only modestly by 2040: there is no mass replacement, technical skills stay relevant and repetitive jobs persist. But benefits stay concentrated in a few sectors, social protection lags and Europe risks stagnation and lost competitiveness.

## Social contract scores (draft)

| Promise | Score | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hard work pays | 3 | Lay-offs and involuntary career changes are limited and technical skills stay relevant, though fear of AI may push wages and conditions down in repetitive-task jobs. |
| Affordable essentials |  | Not addressed: the extract says nothing on the cost of housing, food, energy or care. |
| Reliable safety net | 2 | About 60% of respondents expected social protection to become less effective as union participation falls and non-standard work grows, leaving low-skilled and platform workers exposed. |
| Responsive government | 3 | AI regulation protects citizens and mitigates risks, offset by weaker social dialogue and a missed chance to address climate, cohesion and education. |
| Time for what matters | 3 | Fewer forced career changes and less pressure on working conditions, with purpose-driven careers mattering only to some. |

## Policies from the atlas

- **Regulatory Agencies** (`regulatory-agencies`): AI-related regulation offers a framework that protects individuals as citizens or consumers and addresses legal and ethical considerations, so risks from AI systems are significantly mitigated (p. 46).
- **Workforce Training and Reskilling Investment** (`workforce-training-and-reskilling-investment`): The state bears the larger share of responsibility and costs for broader adult training, especially for less advantaged groups, while firms train mainly their own staff (p. 56).
